description: We're engineering students who love building things that work: code, circuits, and CAD. We bring Java, Verilog, electronics prototyping, and CAD design, and we want to turn a NASA challenge into a real prototype, not just slides. Beginner-friendly but ambitious; everyone owns a real piece of the project. Looking for: Python/data skills, web dev (JS/React), UI/design or video for the pitch, and earth/space science knowledge. No experience needed, just curiosity!
summary:
Trade Space is a browser-based game that lets players design and fly a complete space mission, from concept to closeout. Players choose one of five missions, from Earth orbit to Europa, set a primary science objective, then select instruments, orbit, lifetime, launcher, propulsion, power, communications and shielding. A simulation engine based on simplified real-world physics, including the rocket equation and radio link budgets, instantly shows how each choice affects mass, power, data, cost, and science. The mission then faces build surprises, launch and in-flight anomalies, and only data that reaches Earth counts. A final review explains what helped or hurt and suggests improvements.

Teams of up to four take roles with competing goals and must negotiate and sign off together. Difficulty levels, a sandbox, a tutorial, a field guide and a leaderboard support learners at any level.

Space mission design is usually taught one topic at a time. Trade Space shows how decisions interact across a whole mission, letting students experiment, fail safely, and fly again.
details:
What it does and how it works

Trade Space is a browser game in which players run a complete space mission through the phases NASA uses: concept, design, build and test, launch, operations, and closeout.

  1. Concept: Players choose one of five missions: a wildfire-monitoring satellite in Earth orbit, a lunar ice survey, a Mars climate orbiter, a Vesta asteroid rendezvous,s or a Europa flyby. They set a primary science objective, a team size, and a difficulty.
  2. Design: Players configure instruments, orbit, mission lifetime, trajectory, launch vehicle, propulsion, solar arrays, batteries, radio and antenna, ground stations, data storage, electronics, attitude control, shielding, redundancy, budget reserve,e and the test plan. A simulation engine recalculates the whole spacecraft after every change. It uses the rocket equation for propellant, a radio link budget for data rate, sunlight, which weakens with distance from the Sun, battery drain during eclipses, and radiation dose. Nine status lights flag problems, and a design review blocks plans that break hard limits such as launcher capacity or the budget.
  3. Build and test: Random events, such as late parts, budget cuts,uts or failed analyses, force trade-offs. Mass grows, and the chosen test campaign decides how many hidden defects reach space.
  4. Launch and operations: Players commit to a launch window, then fly the mission cycle by cycle. They manage instrument time and contact with ground stations while handling anomalies. Only data that reaches Earth counts toward the score.
  5. Closeout: A review grades the mission, explains what helped or hurt, shows which single change would most improve the next flight, and produces a mission report.

Benefits

  • Shows the entire mission as a single system: players see how one decision affects many others.
  • Explains its results: status messages and “Show the math” panels use the player’s own numbers to explain why something works or fails.
  • Encourages trying again: players can revise a design and fly it again within minutes.
  • Easy to run: it works in any web browser, offline, with nothing to install, including at phone width.
  • Suits different levels: a tutorial, a field guide of 16 terms, and Trainee, Standard, Expert, and Sandbox difficulties, supporting beginners and experienced players.
  • Supports classrooms and competitions: shared seeds give competing teams identical events, and a leaderboard ranks results.

Intended impact

We want students and aspiring engineers to understand that mission design is about balancing competing demands, not about maximizing a single quantity. Teachers, clubs, and outreach events can run an entire mission in one class period, at no cost and with no special equipment. Team mode is meant to practice the communication and negotiation real mission teams depend on.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with no frameworks. The final game is a single HTML file.
    • A Node.js script combines the source files into the final game.
    • Node.js simulation scripts tuned the difficulty. They searched thousands of random designs per mission and ran 400 simulated flights of each mission’s best design to confirm every mission was winnable but tight.
    • Python’s built-in web server served the game locally for browser testing.
  • Hardware: a standard Windows PC. No special hardware is needed.

Creativity

  • A real engine instead of fixed answers: outcomes come from a physics model, so that players can find their own solutions rather than a single correct path.
  • Hidden defects: cutting the test campaign saves time and money now, but the problems it misses can show up years later in flight.
  • Competing team goals: each role has a goal that conflicts with the others, so players negotiate, and every player signs off at the design review.
  • Only returned data counts: this teaches that collecting data is worthless if the radio can’t send it home.
  • “What if” analysis: the review re-runs the design with single changes and ranks which one would have helped most.
  • Mission control look: status lights, live telemetry, a spacecraft sketch drawn from the actual design, and a mission patch earned at the end.

Factors we considered

  • Realism versus simplicity: we used simplified versions of real equations and real units (km/s, watts, Mbps, krad), explained in plain language. The numbers are teaching approximations, not flight-grade values.
  • Balance: simulation testing sets each mission’s budget so it can succeed, but only with careful trade-offs.
  • Fairness: shared seeds give teams identical events, and Trainee mode removes launch failures for beginners.
  • Collaboration without servers: teams pass a single device around, so the game works anywhere without accounts or internet access.
  • Accessibility: status is shown in both words and color, and controls work via keyboard. The layout fits phones without sideways scrolling, and animations are turned off for players who choose reduced motion.
  • Learning: a first-run tutorial, feedback that explains causes, and the encouragement to fail, learn, and fly again.
